Assignment 1

Assignment 1

Full information online: see Canvas or GitHub.

Overview: select a dataset (you want one that can ask multiple questions), then do some exploratory analyses, and document them.

One minute. The “multiple questions” part matters: a dataset with one response and nothing to group it by will make step 7 hard.

Assignment 1

In this assignment, students will need to:

  1. Select a dataset, provide a description, note where it came from
  2. Read in their dataset
  3. Note the class of the dataset itself (e.g., matrix, list, data frame, etc.)
  4. List the variables of interest and their classes (e.g., numeric, character, etc.)
  5. Examine the structure of the dataset and correct any formatting mistakes
  6. Provide summary statistics for variables of interest
  7. Produce at least 3 different figures that convey different information
  8. For the figures in 7, briefly describe what the figures show

Two minutes. Read it through once; the next slide is the one they will want to photograph.

You already have the tools

Step Where we did it
1. Describe it, cite it READMEs, Lecture 4
2. Read it in Lecture 4: read.csv, read_xlsx
3. Class of the dataset Lecture 4: class()

5. Fix formatting problems Lecture 4: -999. Lecture 5: the kiwi
6. Summary statistics Lecture 4: summary(), table()
7. Three figures Lecture 5: hist, plot, boxplot, barplot

We’re going to get more practice with some of these today as well.

Three minutes. The assignment reads like eight separate tasks and is really a checklist of things they have each done once already. A first assignment always looks bigger than it is, so say that.

Step 5 is worth lingering on. It is the only step with no single function behind it, and it is where the last two lectures both landed: the -999, which you find by reading a README, and the kiwi, which you find by plotting. Steps 6 to 8 we do together later today.

What counts as three different figures

“Three different figures that convey different information”

Three scatterplots of different variables is one kind of figure.

Different information means a different question, e.g.:

Question Plot
How is one variable distributed? hist
How do two relate? plot
How do groups compare? boxplot
How many in each category? barplot

Two minutes. The rubric gives 20% for this, and the obvious failure is three scatterplots with different y variables. The table is Lecture 5’s “Which plot?” table, so this is a callback rather than new material.

The last line is the part nobody thinks of. A student who downloads something from Dryad and reads it out of their Downloads folder has written a script only they can run. Documenting what you did

Open example_R_commented/Example.R

Comments say why, not what:

x <- log10(mass)   # take the log of mass (not great)
x <- log10(mass)   # mass spans 5 orders of magnitude (better)
Shortcut What it does
Ctrl (Cmd) + Shift + R makes a section
Ctrl (Cmd) + Shift + C makes a comment (or comments out highlighted code)
Ctrl (Cmd) + Shift + O opens an outline

Try these commands out.

Three minutes, and this slide is load-bearing: it tells them how the next 40 minutes work. Make the deal explicit: if they keep up, they leave with most of the assignment done.

Give them two or three minutes to open a script and get their data in before moving on, and circulate. Reading in is where the stragglers will be, and it is much cheaper to fix now than in the middle of the next slide.

Assessing many variables at once

Note: if using a different dataset, use your variables.

beak <- avonet[c("Beak.Length_Culmen",
                 "Beak.Length_Nares",
                 "Beak.Width",
                 "Beak.Depth")]
round(cor(beak), 2)

What do these lines of code do?

                   Culmen Nares Width Depth
Beak.Length_Culmen   1.00  0.97  0.74  0.71
Beak.Length_Nares    0.97  1.00  0.73  0.70
Beak.Width           0.74  0.73  1.00  0.91
Beak.Depth           0.71  0.70  0.91  1.00

Three minutes. Ask before clicking. The first line picks four columns by name; the second correlates every column with every other and rounds to two places.

Then ask why Culmen and Nares agree at 0.97. Culmen length is measured from the feathers, Nares length from the nostril: two ways of measuring the same beak. Put both into an analysis and you have counted one measurement twice. This is “identify variables to drop” from the Lecture 5 list, finally shown on the course’s own data.

Remember: they may need use = "complete.obs" for their own dataset if it has NAs. The four beak columns in AVONET have none.

No work pause here. It runs straight into the next slide, and they do both together.

The same thing as a picture

pairs(x = beak,
      pch = 16,
      cex = 0.3,
      col = rgb(red = 0,
                green = 0,
                blue = 0,
                alpha = 0.15)
      )

Same code, different style:

pairs(beak,pch=16,cex=0.3,col=rgb(0,0,0,0.15))

Your turn: try this on your data.

First work pause, about 6 minutes. The number told them there was a problem; the picture tells them what kind. The Culmen/Nares panel is nearly a straight line, visible from across the room, and a picture would also show a curved or clumped relationship that a single correlation flattens into one number.

The two code blocks do the same thing. The first is what we want them writing: one argument per line, named.

Before releasing them: three to five numeric columns, not fifty, or the panels get too small to read. Two things will come up while you circulate: non-numeric columns error, so pick numeric ones, and NAs give a correlation matrix full of NA, which is what use = “complete.obs” is for.

Correlations in your own data

Did anyone find any suspiciously high correlations?

Or anything that might need log-scaling?

Two minutes. Take two or three examples from the room. Most datasets have a redundant pair, and finding it is the point.

Comparing groups

pelicans <- avonet[which(
  avonet$Order1 == "Pelecaniformes"), ]
nrow(pelicans)
boxplot(log10(Mass) ~ Family1,
        data = pelicans)

Check: 110 species, in 5 families

Note the use of which() to select only Pelecaniformes!

Your turn: try a boxplot on your data (figure 1 of 3!)

Photos: Hobbyfotowiki (egret, pelican, hamerkop) and Bildflut (shoebill), CC0; Ron Knight (spoonbill), CC BY 2.0. All via Wikimedia Commons.

Second work pause, about 6 minutes. Calling it “figure 1 of 3” is worth doing: it turns an exercise into visible progress on the assignment.

The photos are in boxplot order, one per family: a great egret (herons), the shoebill, a juvenile brown pelican, two hamerkops, and a roseate spoonbill (ibises and spoonbills). Two of the five boxes are single species, the shoebill and the hamerkop, which is why they are flat lines.

which() and == are from Lecture 4, and the boxplot is Lecture 5’s, applied to a slice rather than the whole dataset. Worth one sentence: this is clunky, and filter() next lecture turns it into one line.

Some students will have no obvious categorical column. Two outs: a character column with a manageable number of values, or come back to this later.

Two plots side by side

carnivores <- avonet[which(
 avonet$Trophic.Level == "Carnivore"), ]
scavengers <- avonet[which(
 avonet$Trophic.Level == "Scavenger"), ]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
 hist(log10(carnivores$Mass),
      main = "Carnivore")
 hist(log10(scavengers$Mass),
      main = "Scavenger")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # put it back!

Three minutes. Two explicit hist() calls, deliberately, not a loop: the loop lands much better later if they have felt the repetition first.

par(mfrow = c(rows, columns)) splits the plotting window, filled row by row.

Warn them about the reset. If they forget par(mfrow = c(1, 1)), every plot for the rest of the session lands in a grid and they will think R is broken.

No work pause yet. Show the trap on the next slide first, so they build the fixed version rather than the broken one.

Look before you believe it

Scavengers look about as common as carnivores.

Read the y axes.

We can sanity check with:

nrow(carnivores)
nrow(scavengers)

Check: 6,115 and 20

Two minutes. The best slide in the block. The bars look the same height because R made them the same height: each panel picked its own y axis. The fix is to set the same ylim in both panels and put n in each title.

The general point is chapter 2’s point: a figure you made yourself can still mislead you. Exploratory graphics are for catching errors, and that includes the errors in your own plot.

Two plots side by side

carnivores <- avonet[which(
 avonet$Trophic.Level == "Carnivore"), ]
scavengers <- avonet[which(
 avonet$Trophic.Level == "Scavenger"), ]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
 hist(log10(carnivores$Mass),
      main = "Carnivore")
 hist(log10(scavengers$Mass),
      main = "Scavenger")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # put it back!

Your turn: plot two groups from your data side by side.

Potential figure 2 of 3.

Third work pause, about 8 minutes. Push them to fix the axes (ylim) and put n in each title, so their version doesn’t have the trap in it.

While you circulate: anyone whose groups are of similar size won’t see the effect. Suggest they pick the commonest and the rarest group, which is where it shows up.

Four groups, four blocks

What about all four groups?

herbivores <- avonet[which(
avonet$Trophic.Level == "Herbivore"), ]
omnivores <- avonet[which(
avonet$Trophic.Level == "Omnivore"), ]

…then four hist() calls, differing by one word each, with ylim written out four times.

What’s the issue with this approach?

Two minutes. Let them answer. The three answers you want: it is tedious, it is easy to mistype one of the four, and if you change your mind about ylim you have to change it in four places. The third is the real one, and it is why professionals avoid copy-paste, not the typing.

For loops

A for() loop does it once.

for (level in c("Carnivore", "Herbivore",
                "Omnivore", "Scavenger")) {
  print(level)
}

Runs the code in { } once per element, setting level to each in turn.

Now we put the plotting code inside!

Two minutes. Run this version on its own first. It takes ten seconds and makes the mechanism visible before any plotting is involved: nearly every loop misunderstanding comes from not seeing that the loop variable changes on each pass.

They will meet a loop again today: section 2.6.2.3 of the R supplement uses one to make small multiples of the seed data. Bolker explains loops in 2.6.1, in the paragraph beginning “for loops are a general way of executing similar commands many times”. We skip the rest of 2.6.1, so point them at that paragraph.

For loops

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (level in c("Carnivore", "Herbivore",
                "Omnivore", "Scavenger")) {
  print(level)
  group_data <- avonet[which(
    avonet$Trophic.Level == level), ]
  hist(log10(group_data$Mass),
       main = level,
       xlab = "log10(Mass)",
       ylim = c(0, 4000), breaks = c(0:6))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Three minutes, demonstration only. Four panels, one copy of the code, one ylim: say that out loud, because it answers the question two slides back.

Now the axes are shared, and the scavengers really do look as rare as they are.

Also worth a sentence: 2.6.2.3 shows a one-line lattice alternative, and Lecture 8 does the same job with facet_wrap(). Three ways to the same figure is normal in R and not something to be anxious about.

Making figures readable

plot(x = log10(avonet$Mass),
     y = log10(avonet$Wing.Length))

Not bad, but could be improved.

How can we see the available arguments for plot()?

Two minutes. The answer: ?plot, which points on to ?par for the graphical settings, plus pressing Tab inside the parentheses in RStudio.

Default labels are the code you typed, which means nothing to a reader. Theirs should be words, with units.

Making figures readable

plot(x = log10(avonet$Mass),
     y = log10(avonet$Wing.Length),
     xlab = "Body mass (log10 g)",
     ylab = "Wing length (log10 mm)",
     main = "Wing length scales with body mass")
fit <- lm(log10(Wing.Length) ~ log10(Mass),
          data = avonet)
abline(fit, col = "red", lwd = 3)

Your turn: make a scatterplot from your own data (potential figure 3 of 3).

Fourth work pause, about 6 minutes, then go back and add labels to figures 1 and 2. This feeds the “figure explanations” 20% directly: a figure whose axes are labeled is most of the way to being explained.

lm() and abline() are from Lecture 3, so the trend line is a callback. The slope is 0.34, worth a passing remark: wing length grows more slowly than mass, which is why big birds look stubby-winged. Don’t chase it. The trend line is optional for their own figures; labels are not.

Saving a figure

png("my_figure.png",
    width = 900, height = 650)
plot(log10(avonet$Mass),
     log10(avonet$Wing.Length))
dev.off()   # nothing is written until this

Nothing appears in the Plots pane. That’s normal.

Your turn: save all three figures. Write a commented-out sentence below the code describing what each plot shows.

About 6 minutes, and the move that turns the work into a deliverable. Everything between png() and dev.off() goes to the file instead of the screen, so the first time they run it they will think nothing happened. Say so before they run it. The file lands in the working directory. The Export button in the Plots pane does the same thing by hand.

Example.R says “in an R file, you can’t save plots the way you can in a .Rmd output”, which raises the question and never answers it. This answers it.

The one-sentence descriptions are Assignment 1 step 8, and writing them now, while the figure is fresh, is far easier than reconstructing the thought later.

End the block by saying what they have: three labeled figures, saved, with descriptions, in a commented script that reads its data from a URL. That is most of Assignment 1.

You want to Use

see how many variables relate, as a picture pairs()
pull out one group data[which(data$column == "value"), ]
compare a number across groups boxplot(y ~ group, data = )
put plots side by side par(mfrow = c(rows, columns)), then put it back
compare panels fairly the same ylim in each, and n in the title
do the same thing for each group for (x in values) { ... }
